# Windmill (`windmill`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by gears_gear_trains, water_wheel
- Core idea: In the European design, sails on a nearly horizontal shaft (tilted up about 10 degrees) face the wind; each sail is a lattice covered with cloth, set at an angle to the plane of rotation and best twisted, steep near the shaft and almost flat at the tip. Sistan mills use a different arrangement: a wall channels the prevailing wind onto one side of a vertical-shaft rotor that can drive a millstone directly. In the European mill, gearing changes the drive direction. To face changing winds the European mill body must turn on a central post (post mill), or only a cap on top of a fixed tower (tower mill). Power rises with the cube of the wind speed and with the sail area, so a mill needs a way to shorten sail and a strong brake. A large mill gives 5 to 10 horsepower in a good wind.
- Pitfalls:
  - Sails set flat-on or at 45 degrees along the whole length; the angle must be small and twisted along the sail
  - No means of turning into the wind; a mill caught tail to wind loses its sails
  - Running away in a gale: the brake overheats and sets the mill on fire, or the stones run dry and spark
  - Assuming windmills are ancient; Greece and Rome did not have them
- History: greece: 1st c. AD – Hero of Alexandria describes a wind wheel working an organ; isolated and its interpretation is disputed; islamic: 9th–10th c. – vertical-shaft mills with walled wind channels in Sistan (al-Mas'udi, al-Istakhri); a story placing them in 644 is a later tradition; europe: c. 1180s – horizontal-shaft post mill, an independent invention (Weedley, Yorkshire 1185; Normandy); tower mills c. 1300; 1745 fantail (Edmund Lee); 1772 spring sails (Meikle); china: 1219 – Yelü Chucai notes windmills in Samarkand; Chinese vertical-shaft mills with sails that feather like a junk's follow, mainly for salt pans and irrigation
- Read:
  - Richard L. Hills, Power from Wind: A History of Windmill Technology (1994)
  - Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962)
  - John Smeaton, An Experimental Enquiry concerning the Natural Powers of Water and Wind to Turn Mills, Phil. Trans. 51 (1759)
